title: Mostly the favourite, sometimes a gamble
allegory: Epsilon-greedy is like eating at your favourite restaurant most nights but rolling a ten-sided die first: on a 1 you try somewhere at random, so a better place can still turn up.

chapters.name: Stuck on a favourite
chapters.note: door A paid once ... so I never opened door B

cap.1: If you always pick whatever has looked best so far, you never find out whether something untried is better. One lucky early result can trap you for good.
cap.2: A purely greedy agent acts on its current Q estimates. Actions it undervalued early are never tried again, so their estimates are never corrected.
cap.3: Q-learning's guarantee needs coverage: every state-action pair keeps being visited. A deterministic greedy behaviour policy can lock onto a worse action permanently.

cap.1: Most nights you eat at your favourite place. But first you roll a ten-sided die, and on a 1 you try somewhere at random. Now and then you find a new favourite.
cap.2: Epsilon-greedy: with probability ε take a uniformly random action, otherwise the action with the highest Q-value. ε = 0.1 means about one random move in ten.
cap.3: π(a|s) = 1 - ε + ε/|A| for the argmax action and ε/|A| for each other action. Every action keeps non-zero probability, which gives learning the coverage it needs.

cap.1: Roll the die. If it says explore, pick any option at random. Otherwise pick the one with the best rating so far. That is the whole rule.
cap.2: With probability ε, env.action_space.sample(); otherwise argmax(Q[s]). The random branch can pick the greedy action too, which is fine.
cap.3: Break ties randomly: with Q initialised to zeros, np.argmax returns action 0 every time, so 'greedy' silently means 'always the first action' until values separate.

curves.label: ε on a linear schedule (example values)

cap.1: At first you know nothing, so explore a lot. As your ratings become trustworthy, roll the die less often. Many setups shrink ε in a straight line, then hold it.
cap.2: In DQN the replay buffer fills with ε-greedy experience while a linear scheduler decays ε: high at the start, a small floor later. The numbers here are examples.
cap.3: Annealing ε trades early coverage for later exploitation; the floor keeps some coverage so estimates for rarely chosen actions can still be corrected.

chapters.name: The cliff edge

right.title: Q-learning (off-policy)
lines: its random slips drop it off

chapters.verdict: Exploration has a price. Whether your values include it is a choice.

cap.1: Walking beside a cliff, a 1-in-10 random step can be fatal. One learner plans around its own clumsiness; the other plans as if it will never slip.
cap.2: On CliffWalking-v0 with ε = 0.1, SARSA prices its random slips into its values and detours (about -17). Q-learning learns the edge path (about -13) but keeps falling in while training.
cap.3: SARSA converges to Q_π for the ε-greedy π it runs; Q-learning to Q*. Prefer SARSA-style values when you will still be exploring at deployment, i.e. when safety matters.

chapters.name: Does ε matter here?
items: Plateau? Ask if exploration is the bottleneck
UCB: explore where you're least sure

cap.1: Some worlds reward almost any poking around; in others, one hidden path decides everything. If your learner stalls, first ask which kind of world it is in.
cap.2: If an agent plateaus, whether ε is the cause depends on the environment's structure, not the algorithm. Its sibling UCB explores where it is most uncertain, not uniformly.
cap.3: Exploration decides which behaviours a learner ever gets to reinforce. In RL fine-tuning of language models, sampling does this job: what is never sampled is never rewarded.

caption.1: Slide ε and the number of options. Watch how long it takes before a dice roll sends you to the gem, and how many nights exploring costs you.
caption.2: A particular untried action is picked with probability ε/n per step, so first contact takes about n/ε steps on average. More options or a smaller ε means slower discovery.
caption.3: P(tried by step t) = 1 - (1 - ε/n)ᵗ. Uniform exploration scales badly with |A|; UCB and optimistic initialisation aim at under-tried actions instead of waiting on luck.

where_else: DQN's replay buffer, filled with ε-greedy experience while ε decays on a linear schedule
Multi-armed bandits, where UCB and Thompson sampling are smarter alternatives
A/B tests and recommender systems that reserve a slice of traffic for trying new options
RL fine-tuning of language models, where sampling decides which behaviours ever get rewarded

hamming.what: A behaviour policy that takes the best-looking action most of the time and a uniformly random one with probability ε.
hamming.when: In value-based RL (SARSA, Q-learning, DQN), whenever the agent must keep trying actions its current estimates undervalue.
hamming.why: Without exploration, early mistakes in the value estimates are never corrected; ε-greedy is the simplest way to keep every action in play.

object.title: The peg tray
object.subtitle: Four situations down the side, five moves across: each peg's height is how often that move gets picked.

knobs.label: ε, chance of a random move
All values start at zero (tie bug)

cap.1: A tray of pegs: four situations down the side, five moves across. One tall peg per row is the current favourite; the short pegs are the dice rolls.
cap.2: π(a|s) for ε-greedy with ε = 0.1 and five actions: 0.92 on the greedy action, 0.02 on each of the others.
cap.3: Greedy action: 1 - ε + ε/|A|. Others: ε/|A|. Every action keeps positive probability.

cap.1: Set ε to zero and the short pegs vanish: pure greed. Anything not already the favourite is never tried again.
cap.2: ε = 0 is a deterministic greedy policy: no coverage, so undervalued actions are never corrected.
cap.3: Without exploration the coverage condition fails, and learning can lock in early estimation errors.

cap.1: Set ε to one and every peg is the same height: pure exploration. You learn about everything but never cash in.
cap.2: ε = 1 is the uniform random policy: maximal coverage, no exploitation.
cap.3: Q-learning can still learn Q* from such data because it is off-policy, but the behaviour itself earns poor return.

cap.1: A classic bug: every value starts at zero, so 'pick the best' quietly means 'pick the first'. The tall pegs all line up in the first column.
cap.2: np.argmax on an all-zero Q returns action 0 every time. Break ties randomly.
cap.3: Deterministic tie-breaking biases early behaviour toward low-index actions until Q separates.

cap.1: In between is the working setting: mostly favourites, enough surprises to keep learning. How much you need depends on the world, not the algorithm.
cap.2: The right ε depends on the environment's structure; decaying schedules start high and settle low.
cap.3: Sparse or deceptive rewards need far more exploration than dense, forgiving ones.

predict.q: ε = 0.1 with 5 actions. How often is the greedy action picked?
predict.why: 90% greedy, plus its share of the random 10%: 0.9 + 0.1/5 = 0.92.

predict.q: Q starts at all zeros and you use np.argmax. What does 'greedy' do at first?
predict.why: np.argmax returns the first maximum, so break ties randomly yourself.

predict.q: Your agent plateaus. Is a higher ε the fix?

options.t: It depends on the environment's structure

predict.why: In some environments any exploration works; in others it decides everything. Diagnose before tuning.
